sections.h2: What is the Green, Ohio housing market like?
sections.html:
Green is a suburban city in southeastern Summit County between Akron and Canton, and it is large by area: about 32 square miles of land, with 1.5 square miles of water. That makes for a spread-out market of subdivisions, lakeside lots and former farm parcels rather than a compact grid.

Green Township was created in 1809 as part of Stark County and joined Summit County when that county formed in 1840. Hamlets such as Greensburg dotted the township, farms gave way to developers after 1950, and voters approved merging the village with the rest of the township in 1991. The city's motto, "A township from the past, a city of the future," reflects that history.

Green uses ZIP codes 44232, 44312, 44319, 44685 and 44216, and some of those addresses are shared with neighboring places. Ask the Summit County Fiscal Office to confirm that your parcel is inside the city limits before you rely on city rules.

sections.h2: What do the Census figures say about homes in Green?
sections.html:
Green's numbers show a settled, owner-heavy suburb. Three in four households own, and the typical owned home is valued at $280,200, while the median household income is $95,047.

The 2020 Census counted 27,475 residents, with a median age of 43.1, and 5.3 percent of its 11,825 housing units were vacant. Census QuickFacts also shows 89.7 percent of residents in the same house a year earlier, a bachelor's degree rate of 42.4 percent, 93.9 percent of households with broadband, and a mean commute of 23.7 minutes. Retail sales reached $1,355,338,000 in 2022, about $49,708 per resident, which reflects the shopping and warehouse activity in the city.

sections.h2: How fast has Green grown, and who lives in its homes?
sections.html:
Green added residents at every count: 22,817 in 2000, 25,699 in 2010 and 27,475 in 2020, with the 2025 estimate at 27,553. Density rose from about 801.7 people per square mile in 2010 to 857.7 in 2020, low enough that lots tend to be larger than in Akron or Canton.

The 2020 Census found 11,195 households, of which 53.8 percent were married couples and 29.7 percent included children under 18. About 26.7 percent were people living alone, and 12.6 percent were someone 65 or older living alone. Those older solo households are the ones most likely to sell a house the family has outgrown, which explains the steady supply of larger homes.

The elevation is about 1,198 feet, and the city is part of the Akron metropolitan area. Sellers outside the area often assume Green is a part of Akron proper, so a listing should name the city and the school district, Green Local Schools, to head off confusion.

sections.h2: What are the zoning and code rules in Green?
sections.html:
The city's Zoning Division issues permits, inspects new structures and enforces the City Code, and it also takes right-of-way applications for aprons and road openings. Its Zoning page lists the most common code complaints:

  • High grass
  • Litter, garbage and debris
  • Junk or inoperable vehicles
  • Storage of RVs, campers and boats
  • Property disrepair

Clearing these before listing avoids a surprise from a buyer's walkthrough. The division is at the Central Administration Building, 1755 Town Park Blvd., and its phone is 330-896-6605. The Land Development Code is in Part Twelve of the city's codified ordinances.

The same page lists the Summit County Department of Building Standards in Akron and Summit County Public Health, at 1867 West Market Street, as the state and county permit and inspection agencies.

sections.h2: What does the Summit County Fiscal Office charge to transfer a Green deed?
sections.html:
The Fiscal Office's fee page lists a conveyance fee of $4.00 per $1,000, rounded up to the next $100 of the sale price, and a lot fee of 50 cents per lot named in the legal description, which applies to exempt and non-exempt transfers alike. That is more than the $3 per $1,000 shown for Hancock and Franklin counties.

Per the Property Transfer page, the department accepts the DTE 100 statement of value or the DTE 100(EX) exemption form, under ORC 319.202 and 319.54(G)(3). Properly prepared forms must reach the Property Transfer Department by 3:30 p.m. to have the legal description approved the same business day.

Recording takes place at the Fiscal Office's Recording Division, 175 South Main Street, 4th floor, Akron. Ohio law (ORC 5301.25) requires a deed to be recorded in the county where the land lies, and an unrecorded deed is treated as fraudulent against a later buyer without notice. Ask the Recording Division for the current per-page recording charge.

sections.h2: Which employers and amenities draw buyers to Green?
sections.html:
Green's 2022 annual financial report, as quoted on Wikipedia, lists Green Local School District as the largest employer with 632 jobs, followed by:

  • Summa Health System, 555
  • Fannie May Confection, 550
  • FedEx Custom Critical, 495
  • Diebold Nixdorf, 427
  • Target, 369

Interstate 77 serves the city, and the Akron-Canton Regional Airport lies partly inside Green and partly in Jackson Township. Green opened the first two-lane roundabout in Summit County in 2009 and had 11 roundabouts as of 2024.

Boettler Park, a 26-acre park with trails, fishing, picnicking and biking, and the Singer Lake Bog nature preserve are public spaces in the city. Public school students attend Green Local Schools. A mayor and a seven-member council run the city, with four of the council members chosen by ward and everyone limited to two consecutive four-year terms.

sections.h2: What should a Green seller know about pipelines and local history?
sections.html:
Green fought the NEXUS Pipeline in court starting in 2016 because the line runs near residential neighborhoods, wetlands and the Comet Lake Dam. Construction began in 2018 after the city reached a $7.5 million settlement. If your lot is near the route, check your title paperwork for any easement before a buyer asks.

From about 1950 farmers began selling land to developers, so Green houses range from older farm properties to newer subdivision homes.

sections.h2: Which sale routes work for a Green house on a deadline?
sections.html:
• Agent listing: a fit for move-in-ready homes where recent nearby sales give a clear price.
  • Investor sale: suited to dated houses, open code complaints, or an estate sale on a deadline.
  • Owner sale: saves commission but requires you to prepare the DTE 100 and deed paperwork.

Whichever route you pick, price the house against nearby Green sales, check for open zoning complaints, and gather the survey, title and any septic records.

faqs.q: Who handles building permits for a Green house?
faqs.a: The City of Green Zoning Division issues zoning permits and does inspections of new structures, while the Summit County Department of Building Standards and Summit County Public Health handle county and state level building and health matters.

faqs.q: What does Summit County charge to transfer a Green deed?
faqs.a: The Fiscal Office lists $4.00 per $1,000 of sale price, rounded up to the next $100, plus 50 cents per lot. Forms received by 3:30 p.m. can be approved the same day.

faqs.q: Where is a Green deed recorded?
faqs.a: At the Summit County Fiscal Office Recording Division, 175 South Main Street, 4th floor, Akron. Ohio law puts the filing in the county where the land lies.

faqs.q: Who are the largest employers in Green?
faqs.a: Per the city's 2022 financial report as quoted on Wikipedia, Green Local School District leads with 632 employees, followed by Summa Health System, Fannie May Confection and FedEx Custom Critical.

faqs.q: Where do I check for zoning violations before listing a Green house?
faqs.a: Call the Zoning Division at 330-896-6605. Its page lists high grass, litter, junk vehicles, stored RVs and boats, and property disrepair as the most common complaints.
